A caldera is a large, bowl-shaped hollow in the ground formed when a volcano partially collapses into itself after a massive eruption.

Deep beneath a volcano lies a chamber filled with molten rock called magma. Think of it like a giant underground balloon full of lava. When a powerful eruption occurs, enormous amounts of this magma are blasted out. The chamber empties — or empties enough — and the roof of that chamber (the ground above it) no longer has anything supporting it from below. So it caves in, like a ceiling with no pillars. The result is a massive, wide, basin-shaped depression on the surface. That depression is a caldera.
How is it different from a crater?

People often confuse these two, so this distinction is important.

A crater is the small, funnel-shaped opening at the top of a volcano's vent — the "mouth" through which lava and gases escape. It forms because of the eruption itself — material is blasted away or builds up around the vent. Craters are typically small, usually measuring tens to a few hundred metres across.

A caldera is entirely different in origin and scale. It does not form because material is blasted away. It forms because the ground collapses downward after the underground chamber drains. Calderas are vastly larger — they range from about 1 kilometre to over 100 kilometres across. Some are so large that you cannot see across them. In fact, if you stood in the middle of a large caldera, you might not even realize you were inside one — it looks more like a wide, flat valley ringed by mountains than a traditional volcano.

The simplest way to remember the difference: a crater is a hole punched out; a caldera is a ceiling that caved in.

Calderas vary enormously in size. A small caldera might be just a kilometre or two wide. But some calderas are staggering in scale:

  • The Yellowstone Caldera in the United States measures roughly 55 × 72 kilometres. It is so large that most of Yellowstone National Park sits inside it.
  • The Toba Caldera in Indonesia is about 100 × 30 kilometres. It formed from one of the largest eruptions in Earth's history (roughly 74,000 years ago) and now contains a large lake.
  • Santorini in Greece is a caldera — the famous crescent-shaped island and the sea bay in the middle are the remnants of a volcano that partially collapsed thousands of years ago.
What forms inside a caldera over time?

Because calderas are large, deep depressions, many things can develop inside them:

  • Lakes: Rainwater and groundwater collect in the basin, forming caldera lakes. One famous example is Crater Lake in Oregon, USA — confusingly named, it is actually a caldera, not a crater. It formed when a volcano called Mount Mazama collapsed about 7,700 years ago. The lake is over 590 metres deep.
  • New volcanic vents: Even after the collapse, volcanic activity doesn't always stop. New smaller cones or vents can emerge from the floor of the caldera. The small island called Wizard Island, visible inside Crater Lake, is one such new cone.
  • Geothermal features: Hot springs, geysers, and fumaroles (vents releasing steam and gas) are common inside active calderas. Yellowstone's famous geysers, including Old Faithful, are a direct result of the volcanic heat still present beneath its caldera.
  • Resurgence: In some calderas, magma slowly refills the chamber below, pushing the caldera floor upward again over thousands of years. This creates a dome-shaped bulge in the middle, and such calderas are called resurgent calderas.

Yes — directly. The term supervolcano describes a volcano capable of producing an eruption of extreme, catastrophic scale. Nearly every supervolcano has a caldera, because eruptions powerful enough to earn the "super" label are exactly the kind that drain the magma chamber and cause a massive collapse. Yellowstone and Toba are both considered supervolcanoes, and both are identified by their calderas.

When geologists look for ancient supervolcanoes, the presence of a caldera (especially a very large one) is one of the primary clues they look for.
Can a caldera be active and dangerous?

Yes, absolutely. A caldera being there doesn't mean the volcano is dead. Many calderas sit above magma chambers that are still partially full and slowly recharging. Signs that a caldera is restless include:

  • Ground deformation: The floor of the caldera slowly rises or falls as magma moves below.
  • Earthquake swarms: Small, frequent earthquakes caused by underground movement of magma or fluids.
  • Increased geothermal activity: More steam, new hot springs, or higher temperatures in existing ones.

For example, Campi Flegrei (meaning "burning fields") near Naples, Italy, is an active caldera that has shown measurable ground uplift for decades and is closely monitored. Yellowstone is also monitored continuously, though scientists consider a large eruption there unlikely in the near future.

A caldera is a large, basin-like depression formed when a volcano's underground magma chamber empties during a major eruption and the overlying ground collapses inward. It is not the same as a crater (which is simply a volcano's vent opening). Calderas can be many kilometres wide, can contain lakes, new volcanic vents, and geothermal features, and they are the defining feature of supervolcanoes. Some calderas are extinct and peaceful; others are still geologically active and are watched carefully by scientists.
